$comment: A DELIBERATELY WRONG manifest, for one property only: the bound on the wait for the
run's terminal is a FINDING when it is hit, never a skip and never a pass.
Steps 1 and 2 are the real ones and must pass. Step 3 declares a bound of 1 ms, which
no real run can meet, and the journey must exit 1 saying so and printing every reading
it took before the bound.
npm --prefix web run e2e:pc01 -- --origin http://ORIGIN --phase write \
--manifest ../tests/e2e/pc01/journey/fixtures/redden-write-bound.manifest.json
It also declares the 202 as a 200 and `state` as `published` rather than `queued`, so
the same run proves the status and response-body checks on the call D-5 actually was.
The sign-in and the declared viewport are copied from the real manifest by
`W44-JOURNEY`. They are NOT what this fixture is demonstrating: it demonstrates the
findings below, and since D-92 every manifest needs a session to reach any screen at
all. A fixture without one would redden for the wrong reason and prove nothing.

$comment: The WRITE half of the journey. `D-30`, and before it `D-5`.
`D-5` was `POST /api/v1/runs` -> 500, twice, through a browser, on 2026-09-16. The
read walk above would not have caught it: it makes no POST. These three steps do what
a user does -- name a project and press Create, choose the AR PDF and press Upload,
press Start run -- through the app's own controls, on the public origin.
Read by the same two checkers as `routes`. At RUN TIME `write.mjs` presses these
controls and asserts the request, the status, the response body and what the screen
rendered afterwards. At GATE TIME the conformance guard asserts that every
`page_module` and `control_module` exists, that each step's `at` is a route the read
walk also covers, that every (method, path, operationId) triple is a real contract
operation, that the fixture is on disk, and that every selector, text and marker
attribute named here still appears in `web/src`.
That last check is new. `W21-E2E` stated the guard's cost as 'it checks addressing,
not behaviour'. The write half's handles are not addressing, so leaving them unguarded
would have meant a renamed id turns the journey red only when someone runs it. The
check is still not behaviour -- it proves the handle exists in the source, not that
pressing it does anything -- and that residue is stated rather than closed.
`%STAMP%` is replaced with the run's UTC timestamp. The app mints its idempotency key
from the typed name, so a fixed name would make every run the same command and the
second run of the day would assert nothing about creation.

capture.$why: the screen states what it created, in its own role=status line
on success the screen navigates to the published version's own address
the 202 reading carries the run, and the screen moves to run progress

$comment: The run reaches its terminal asynchronously. This does NOT sleep: it reads
the attribute the run screen's own poller writes, and that poller is the
application's single `pollRunStatus` loop at its frozen 2s/x1.5/15s schedule.
`bound_ms` is this journey's bound, not the app's -- `polling.ts` deliberately
has no deadline. Reaching the bound is a finding with every reading attached,
and exit 1. It is never a skip and never a pass.

write.$why_the_labels_were_corrected: W44-JOURNEY 2026-09-24. These steps pressed controls labelled Create, Upload and Start run. The application was translated and says Создать, Загрузить and Запустить прогон, so this fixture died at the first click and produced findings about a control it could not press INSTEAD of the deliberate wrongs it declares -- 5 findings where the README documents 6, and 4 where it documents 4 but for different reasons. A proof that fails for an accidental reason has stopped proving what it says it proves. The real manifest did not rot because make gate reads it (test_every_control_the_write_half_presses_still_exists_in_the_application); fixtures are not read by that guard, by design, so their deliberate wrongs never redden the gate -- and that is also why nothing caught this.
